study_identification.title: Brain charts for the human lifespan

study_characteristics.study_objective: To create interactive brain growth charts to benchmark brain morphology across the lifespan by aggregating the largest neuroimaging dataset to quantify individual differences in brain structure relative to normative trajectories, and to demonstrate their utility in identifying neurodevelopmental milestones and quantifying brain structure atypicality in neurological and psychiatric disorders.
study_characteristics.study_design_other: The study primarily used cross-sectional data from 100+ primary studies to establish normative trajectories. Approximately 10% of the dataset included longitudinal scans (N=9,306 scans from 41 studies) which were used to assess stability of centile scores over time, not to fit the models.

dataset_name.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (UK Biobank; ABCD; HCP; IMAGEN; ADNI; ABIDE; ADHD-200; Developing Human Connectome Project; CALM; Cam-CAN; FinnBrain; HABS; NSPN; POND; and 100+ other studies)

hc_n.answer: Total scans: 123,984 MRI scans; Total participants: 101,457 participants. The exact number of healthy controls after exclusions is reported per phenotype in Supplementary Table 1.2-1.42. Models were built on healthy controls only, with clinical cases analyzed separately.

hc_age.answer: Age range: 115 days post-conception (approximately -0.38 years relative to birth) to 100 years of age. Specific age ranges per phenotype are detailed in Supplementary Tables 1.2-1.42.

hc_sex.answer: Sex distribution varies by study and phenotype. Models were sex-stratified with separate trajectories for males and females. Specific N and percentages per phenotype reported in Supplementary Tables 1.2-1.42. Note: Males have larger brain-tissue volumes than females in absolute terms.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer (~95% of reference dataset); Infant FreeSurfer; NEOCIVET (for neonatal data); Software version included as covariate (5 categories)

quality_checking_detail.answer: Multiple complementary QC approaches: (1) Euler Index (EI) filtering - analyzed N=101,708 scans on N=82,023 subjects; sensitivity analysis excluded scans with EI > 2 median absolute deviations from study-specific median (~9-10% of scans); models highly robust to EI filtering (all R² > 0.999). (2) Expert visual quality control - N=9,704 scans rated on 6-point scale; only 3% (N=374) assigned to worst quality categories (5-6); models robust after excluding poor quality scans (R² > 0.999). (3) Study-specific QC - each primary study conducted their own QC procedures. (4) Test-retest reliability - validated on N=72 scans from test-retest dataset.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: GAMLSS framework included study-specific random effects for both mean (μ) and variance (σ) parameters to account for site/study-specific batch effects. This approach: (1) included study as a random effect in the model estimation, (2) included preprocessing pipeline (5 categories) as a fixed effect, (3) provided study-specific offsets that allowed for harmonization across technically diverse studies, (4) enabled out-of-sample data from new studies to be aligned using maximum likelihood estimation of study-specific random effects. Compared to ComBat in Supplementary Information 5.

modeling_method.answer: GAMLSS (Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape)

software_tool.answer: R GNU v4.1.2; GAMLSS R package; ggplot; raincloudplots; ComplexHeatmap; lmerTest; ggstatsplot; effsize; Interactive tool at www.brainchart.io; Code available at https://github.com/brainchart/Lifespan

response_variable.answer: Primary cerebrum tissue volumes (bilateral): Total cortical grey matter volume (GMV); Total white matter volume (WMV); Total subcortical grey matter volume (sGMV); Ventricular cerebrospinal fluid volume (Ventricles/CSF). Extended phenotypes: Total cerebrum volume (TCV); Total surface area (SA); Mean cortical thickness (CT); Regional cortical volumes (34 bilateral regions from Desikan-Killiany parcellation)

predictor_variables.answer: Age (fractional polynomials); Sex (binary: male/female); Study (random effect); Preprocessing pipeline/software version (5 categories)

predictor_effects.answer: Fixed effects: Intercept; Sex (female or male); Software version (5 categories); Age (fractional polynomials of varying orders). Random effects: Study-specific random intercepts for μ (mean) component; Study-specific random intercepts for σ (variance) component (for most phenotypes); Random effects drawn from normal distribution with zero mean and variance to be estimated: γ ~ N(0, δ²). Model specification per phenotype: GMV, sGMV, WMV used 3rd order fractional polynomials for μ and 2nd order for σ with study random effects for both μ and σ; Ventricles used 3rd order fractional polynomials for μ and 3rd order for σ with study random effect for μ only; ν (skewness) component used intercept only (no age or random effects).

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly handled nuisance variables through multiple mechanisms in the GAMLSS framework: (1) study-specific random effects for both mean and variance parameters to account for site/batch effects, (2) preprocessing pipeline as a fixed effect covariate with 5 categories, (3) sex-stratified models, and (4) extensive quality control procedures including Euler Index filtering and expert visual QC.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: In short, using a sex-stratified approach, age, preprocessing pipeline and study were each included in the GAMLSS model estimation of first order (μ) and second order (σ) distribution parameters of a generalized gamma distribution using fractional polynomials to model nonlinear trends... For each component of the generalized gamma distribution, α terms correspond to fixed effects of the intercept, sex (female or male), and software version used for pre-processing (five categories); β terms correspond to the fixed effects of age, modelled as fractional polynomial functions with the number of terms reflecting the order of the fractional polynomials; and γ terms correspond to the study-level random effects.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main paper lines 421-444; Supplementary Information Section 5 'Batch correction and site harmonisation'

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason:
The study performed extensive within-sample validation using leave-one-study-out (LOSO) analyses, where normative trajectories were repeatedly estimated after iteratively excluding each of the 100+ primary studies. This constitutes validation on same-domain (structural MRI) data that is non-independent (from the same aggregated reference dataset). Additionally, bootstrap resampling procedures were used for model validation.
EXTRAS: {"details": "LOSO analyses performed for all 100+ studies; Bootstrap analyses with stratified resampling by study and sex; Model stability assessed across all LOSO iterations; Trajectories highly conserved after exclusion of each individual study; Statistics reported in Supplementary Table 7 (ST7.1-7.7)"}
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Extensive jack-knife and leave-one-study-out analyses indicated that a study size of N > 100 scans was sufficient for stable and unbiased estimation of out-of-sample centile scores (Supplementary Information 4)... The reliability of the models was assessed and endorsed by cross-validation and bootstrap resampling procedures (Supplementary Information 3)... To test whether our model's reliability was skewed toward any particular study, we performed a leave-one-study-out (LOSO) analysis. Specifically, we iteratively subsetted our dataset, leaving out one study, re-estimated all model parameters and extracted the fitted trajectories.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main paper lines 107, 419; Supplementary Methods Section 3.2.1 'Leave-one-study-out' (lines 494-499), Section 3.2.2 'Bootstrap analysis'

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason:
The study validated the models using multiple independent same-domain (structural MRI) datasets not included in the reference dataset: (1) test-retest dataset (N=72 scans) for reliability assessment, (2) external validation against non-imaging metrics (brain weight data, ultrasound measurements, head circumference from WHO and other sources), and (3) heritability validation in two independent twin studies (ABCD and HCP, total N=913 twin pairs).
EXTRAS: {"details": "Test-retest dataset: N=72 scans, validated reliability of out-of-sample centile scoring (ICC >0.91-0.98 depending on motion correction); Twin heritability validation: ABCD and HCP datasets, N=913 twin pairs total; External non-MRI validation datasets listed in Supplementary Information Section 20: Brain weight data, Ultrasound datasets (Hsu et al., Chang et al., Roelfsema et al.), WHO postnatal head circumference, International prenatal head circumference; Cross-validation with non-imaging metrics showed high correspondence"}
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Out-of-sample centile scores proved highly reliable in multiple test-retest datasets and were robust to variations in image processing pipelines (Supplementary Information 4)... Recognising that image quality would likely be most influential for out-of-sample centile scoring of scans that were not included in the reference dataset, we analysed N=72 scans from an open test-retest dataset which had been quantitatively QC'd (by 5 independent raters using Braindr) but had not previously been included in our analysis... Centile scores also showed increased twin-based heritability in two independent studies (total N = 913 twin pairs) compared with non-centiled phenotypes (average increase of 11.8 percentage points in narrow sense heritability (h²) across phenotypes; Fig. 4d, Supplementary Information 13).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Main paper lines 99, 107-108; Supplementary Methods Section 2.3 'Image quality and out-of-sample centile scoring' (line 454), Section 3.4 'Brain weight, ultrasound, and head circumference validation', Section 13 'Twin-based heritability', Section 20 'Replication/validation datasets'

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason:
The study validated MRI-derived centile scores against different domain data including: (1) non-imaging developmental metrics (resting metabolic rate, motor milestone acquisition, height/weight growth curves, pubertal development), (2) birth outcomes data (gestational age and birth weight in 5 primary studies), and (3) brain weight from postmortem data spanning different ages.
EXTRAS: {"details": "Different domain validation data included: (1) Birth outcomes (5 studies): gestational age and birth weight significantly associated with centile scores; (2) Resting metabolic rate (RMR): minimum at 7 months, maximum at 4.2 years; (3) Motor milestones: WHO gross motor development milestones; (4) Anthropometric growth: height and weight velocity curves; (5) Pubertal development: Tanner scale ranges; (6) Brain weight postmortem data; (7) Head circumference (WHO postnatal, international prenatal standards)"}
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Comparing these models with multiple non-MRI metrics of brain size demonstrated high correspondence across the lifespan (Supplementary Information 3)... In five primary studies covering the lifespan, average centile scores across global tissues were related to two metrics of premature birth (gestational age at birth: t = 13.164, P < 2 × 10⁻¹⁶; birth weight: t = 36.395, P < 2 × 10⁻¹⁶; Supplementary Information 12), such that greater gestational age and birth weight were associated with higher average centile scores... To further contextualize the neuroimaging trajectories, diagnostic age ranges from previous literature (blue boxes in Fig. 3) were compared with empirical age ranges of patients... Developmental milestones were also compared to published work for brain resting metabolic rate, from its minimum in infancy to its maximum in early childhood; anthropometric variables (height and weight), which reach a first peak in velocity during infancy and a second peak in velocity in adolescence; typical acquisition of the six gross motor capabilities; and pubertal age ranges.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Main paper lines 61-62 (Fig 3 legend), 98-99, 469; Supplementary Information Section 3.4 'Brain weight, ultrasound, and head circumference validation', Section 12 'Associations of birth weight and gestational duration with centile scores'

clinical_dataset.answer: Clinical cases were included within the aggregated dataset from the same 100+ primary studies. Major clinical datasets contributing cases included: ADNI (Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) for AD and MCI; ABIDE (Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange) for ASD; ADHD-200 for ADHD; BSNIP (Bipolar & Schizophrenia Consortium) for BD and SCZ; IMAGEN for various psychiatric conditions; POND for neurodevelopmental disorders; and many others (see Supplementary Information 19)

diseases_studied.answer: Alzheimer's disease (AD); Mild cognitive impairment (MCI); Frontotemporal dementia (FTD); Lewy body dementia (LBD); Parkinson's disease (PD); Autism spectrum disorder (ASD); Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD); Schizophrenia (SCZ); Bipolar disorder (BD); Major depressive disorder (MDD); Anxiety or phobic disorders (ANX); Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD)

clinical_groups_n.answer: Analysis was stratified by sample size thresholds: Large groups (N > 500) for AD, MCI, SCZ, ASD, ADHD, and others presented in Fig. 4a and Supplementary Tables 3.1-3.7; Medium groups (N > 250) in Supplementary Tables 3.8-3.14; Smaller groups (N > 100) in Supplementary Tables 3.15-3.21; Smallest groups (N > 50) in Supplementary Tables 3.22-3.28. Longitudinal data: N = 9,306 scans from 41 studies. Groups with diagnostic changes (e.g., MCI to AD) were analyzed separately.

clinical_groups_age.answer: Age distributions varied by disorder and corresponded to typical age of onset/diagnosis: Neurodevelopmental disorders (ASD, ADHD) predominantly childhood through adolescence; Mood/anxiety disorders predominantly adolescence through adulthood; Neurodegenerative disorders (AD, MCI, PD) predominantly older adults (>60 years); Schizophrenia/Bipolar predominantly young adulthood through middle age. Specific age ranges per clinical group are detailed in Supplementary Tables 3.1-3.28. The largest case-control differences across epochs occurred in late adulthood when risk for dementia increases and in adolescence, which is well-recognized as a period of increased incidence of mental health disorders.

clinical_groups_sex.answer: Analyses were sex-stratified throughout. Specific sex distributions per clinical group are reported in Supplementary Tables 3.1-3.28 and demographic tables ST1.2-1.42. Sex differences in centile scores within clinical cohorts were analyzed (Supplementary Table 8, ST8.1-8.7). Notable finding: Alzheimer's disease showed greatest overall difference, with maximum difference localized to grey matter volume in biologically female patients (median centile score = 14%, 36 percentage points difference from CN median, corresponding to Cohen's d = 0.88).

deviation_metric.answer: Primary deviation metrics: (1) Centile scores - individual scans quantified as percentile position (0-1 or 0-100) on age- and sex-stratified normative distributions for each MRI phenotype using inverse cumulative density function F⁻¹ with model parameters and individual's data; (2) Centile Mahalanobis Distance (CMD) - multivariate metric combining centile scores across multiple MRI phenotypes to provide aggregate atypicality measure, calculated as Mahalanobis distance in 4-dimensional feature space relative to normative mean, equivalent to sum of squares of standardized principal component scores.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Multiple statistical approaches: (1) Case-control comparisons using bootstrapped (500 bootstraps) non-parametric generalization of Welch's one-way ANOVA; Pairwise, sex-stratified post-hoc comparisons using Monte Carlo permutation tests (10,000 permutations); FDR correction via Benjamini-Hochberg at q < 0.05 across all case-control pairs within sex and feature; Cohen's d effect sizes calculated; Results in Supplementary Tables 3.1-3.28. (2) Longitudinal stability assessed via interquartile range (IQR) of centile scores across timepoints; Groups with N ≥ 50 longitudinal subjects analyzed; Diagnostic progression (e.g., MCI to AD) analyzed separately; Results in Supplementary Tables 5-6. (3) Cross-diagnostic analyses via hierarchical clustering of multivariate centile score profiles and sliding window analyses of cross-disorder discriminability; Results in Supplementary Information 11. (4) Dimensional associations including birth outcomes (gestational age: t=13.164, P<2×10⁻¹⁶; birth weight: t=36.395, P<2×10⁻¹⁶), heritability via twin-based ACE models comparing centiled vs. raw phenotypes, and sex effects via linear models within clinical cohorts (Supplementary Table 8).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Brain charts revealed previously unreported neurodevelopmental milestones, showed high longitudinal stability, increased heritability compared to raw phenotypes, and demonstrated significant case-control differences across neurological and psychiatric disorders with Alzheimer's disease showing the largest deviations.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The study identified multiple novel neurodevelopmental milestones including: GMV peak at 5.9 years (95% CI: 5.8-6.1, 2-3 years later than previous reports), WMV peak at 28.7 years (CI: 28.1-29.2), sGMV peak at 14.4 years (CI: 14.0-14.7), cortical thickness peak at 1.7 years (CI: 1.3-2.1), and a period of GMV:WMV differentiation from 1 month to 3 years. Regional cortical volumes showed heterochronicity, with primary sensory regions peaking earliest (~2 years) and fronto-temporal association cortex peaking latest (~10 years). Case-control analyses (N>500 per group) revealed significant differences across disorders with effect sizes ranging from medium (0.2 < d < 0.8) to large (d > 0.8). Alzheimer's disease showed the greatest deviation (median centile=14%, 36 percentage points from controls, d=0.88 in females for GMV). Schizophrenia ranked third on CMD behind AD and MCI. Hierarchical clustering identified three disorder clusters: neurodegenerative, mood/anxiety, and neurodevelopmental. Centile scores showed 11.8 percentage point average increase in heritability compared to raw volumes across 913 twin pairs. Birth weight and gestational age significantly predicted centile scores across the lifespan (both P<2×10⁻¹⁶). Longitudinal stability was high (median IQR<0.05) with increased variability during diagnostic transitions (e.g., MCI to AD).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Major limitations include: (1) bias toward European and North American populations and European ancestry groups, (2) unequal age distribution with under-representation of foetal, neonatal, and mid-adulthood (30-40 years) epochs, (3) variability in diagnostic criteria and ascertainment across primary studies that cannot be fully corrected, (4) out-of-sample centile scoring requires N>100 scans for stability and is not yet validated for individual clinical diagnosis, (5) sex was treated as binary without dimensional gender self-report, and (6) quality control importance remains paramount especially for finer-grained phenotypes.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Notable innovations and applications: (1) Interactive web tool at www.brainchart.io allows users to visualize demographics and normative trajectories interactively, explore case-control differences across diagnostic categories, compute out-of-sample centile scores for new datasets (N≥100), and access without data-sharing hurdles or computational barriers. (2) Out-of-sample estimation via maximum likelihood estimation of study-specific random effects for new data conditional on fitted model, avoiding need to refit entire model or share reference data. (3) Open science resources including code at https://github.com/brainchart/Lifespan and publicly available model parameters and centile scoring tools. (4) Scale-invariant CMD generalizable to additional MRI phenotypes as they are added in future. (5) Models remarkably robust to image quality variation, processing pipeline differences, and study exclusion (all LOSO correlations R²>0.999). (6) Clinical translation demonstrated via diagnostic transition tracking (MCI to AD), trans-diagnostic comparisons, and developmental milestone identification. (7) Planned iterative updates as additional data become available.
